title: TikTok Events API: fields, deduplication and validation
summary: Learn the TikTok Events API event structure, server-side setup, Pixel deduplication with event_id and how to validate conversion signals.
body_markdown:
The most common TikTok Events API advice stops at one step: send the same` event_id` from the browser and the server. The rule is right. It still has to be tested against retries, delayed events and source changes, with an expected conversion count.


A stronger approach starts with **one conversion contract** . Define the event name, value, currency, transaction identity and` event_id` rule before building the integration. Then use a test matrix to check whether TikTok receives the conversion you intended, without counting another copy or losing the event.


## What the TikTok Events API covers


The TikTok Events API is a secure server-to-server integration that sends customer actions to TikTok from websites, mobile apps, offline systems and CRM platforms.


A purchase doesn't always finish inside a browser session. A customer may place an order by phone, complete registration in an app or become a qualified lead after a sales call. A backend or CRM can report those outcomes even when browser tracking is incomplete or unavailable.


According to[TikTok's Events API documentation](https://business-api.tiktok.com/portal/docs/events-api-for-web/v1.3) , **Events API 2.0** uses` /event/track/` and unifies the supported sources under one schema. TikTok recommends this version for new integrations and recommends upgrading existing Events API 1.0 implementations.


### Choose the source that describes the action


The` event_source` field tells TikTok where the reported action belongs:


- **` web`** describes a website linked to a TikTok Pixel Code, typically reporting actions such as` ViewContent` or` Purchase` .
- **` app`** describes a mobile app, typically reporting actions such as` Purchase` or` CompleteRegistration` . Sending app events through Events API 2.0 is allowlist-only, so ask your TikTok representative first.
- **` offline`** describes store or phone sales uploaded after the transaction. It takes standard events only, typically` Purchase` .
- **` crm`** describes a lead outcome in a CRM system, such as a qualified lead. It takes custom events only.


These source values describe the event's origin. They aren't labels for transport methods. A website purchase sent by your backend is still a web event, not an offline event merely because a server delivered it.


### Use one model without erasing source differences


A shared schema means your team doesn't need separate definitions of order value for the storefront, app and sales export. Each pipeline can map its records into the same conversion contract.


That doesn't mean every source needs identical customer identifiers. A store sale may lack browser context. A CRM record may contain a stored click ID but no current page URL. Preserve the fields that exist rather than fabricating browser information.


Separate **business facts** from **delivery context** . The purchase amount belongs to the transaction. The source and permitted match keys describe how that transaction reaches TikTok.


List the sources your business already sends. For each, name the system that creates the event, the person who owns it and any conversion outcomes that aren't reported.


Mark those gaps before changing tags. Otherwise, you can spend a release fixing browser purchases while leaving qualified leads or store sales outside the measurement process.


## Event structure and required fields


Every request identifies its` event_source` and carries a` data` array of up to 1,000 event objects.` event_source_id` names what measures the events: the Pixel Code for web, the TikTok App ID for app, the Offline Event Set ID for offline and the CRM Event Set ID for CRM. Web events also carry a` page` object with the URL where the event happened. Each event needs an exact` event` name and an` event_time` expressed as Unix time in UTC seconds, as defined in[TikTok's parameter documentation](https://business-api.tiktok.com/portal/docs/parameters/v1.3) .


**Events API 2.0 payload fields**


Field Required Format Example value


` event_source` Yes` web` ,` app` ,` offline` or` crm`` web`


` event_source_id` Yes Pixel Code, TikTok App ID, Offline Event Set ID or CRM Event Set ID Your Pixel Code


` data` Yes Array of event objects, up to 1,000 per request One or more events per request


` event` Yes Case-sensitive standard or custom name` Purchase`


` event_time` Yes Unix timestamp in UTC seconds Original transaction time converted to UTC seconds


` event_id` When the Pixel and the Events API send the same web event Unique per event, identical across Pixel and server copies Persisted purchase-event ID


` page.url` Yes for web URL where the event happened The confirmation page URL


` properties.value` Recommended for revenue events Number, without currency symbols Saved order total


` properties.currency` Recommended with value ISO 4217 code` USD`


` properties.contents\[\].content_id` Recommended Product ID, ideally the catalog's SKU or item group ID Storefront product identifier


` properties.content_type` Recommended` product` or` product_group`` product`


The example cells describe payload values, not production defaults. Replace the Pixel Code and product identifier with actual records. The table is a field checklist, not a flat JSON template: request fields, event fields and commerce properties belong at their documented nesting levels.


` event_id` appears here so it isn't missed during implementation. Its identity rules belong with deduplication, including server retries, rather than basic request validation.


### Prevent timestamp and commerce errors


**Milliseconds aren't seconds.** Many application logs and date libraries represent time in milliseconds. Sending that representation unchanged can place the event far into the future instead of at the transaction time.


Keep the original occurrence time when a queue delays delivery. A retry should not make yesterday's purchase look like a new purchase made when the worker restarted.


**Value needs a currency.** A numeric amount alone doesn't identify its monetary unit. Check the pair before transmission, and define whether your purchase value includes tax, shipping and discounts.


That definition belongs in the conversion contract. Don't let the browser send a checkout subtotal while the backend sends the final charged amount.


**Product identifiers need a shared reference.** Take` content_id` from the same product system used by the storefront and product feed. A display label, internal database key and catalog identifier may all describe the same item, but they aren't interchangeable.


### Validate meaning as well as format


A request can have valid types and still describe the wrong action. A number in` value` passes a type check even if it contains the basket subtotal from before a discount.


Build checks at both levels:


- **Schema checks** confirm required fields, types, nesting and permitted source values.
- **Business checks** compare the payload with the saved transaction, including amount, currency and product identity.
- **Delivery checks** connect the outgoing request and response to the event record.


Before a release, send a test request and read back every field. Compare it with the saved order and this checklist, not just the success status.


## Standard event names and case matching


` purchase` is not` Purchase` . That difference matters even when your server successfully reaches TikTok's endpoint.


**Standard events** use names TikTok documents for recognized actions. **Custom events** describe actions for which your implementation uses its own name. A custom label isn't an alias that automatically becomes the nearest standard event.


[TikTok's supported-events documentation](https://business-api.tiktok.com/portal/docs/supported-events/v1.3) requires exact spelling and capitalization for standard event names. A mismatch can stop TikTok from treating a received hit as the intended standard event.


**Standard event names and common wrong variants**


Standard event Usual trigger Common wrong variant


` Purchase` Order confirmed on the server` purchase`


` AddToCart` Product added to the basket` add_to_cart`


` ViewContent` Product detail page loaded` viewcontent`


` CompleteRegistration` Sign-up confirmed` completeregistration`


### Translate internal names at the boundary


Your application may use` add_to_cart` in the` dataLayer` or an internal event bus. That's not necessarily a problem. The problem appears when the TikTok adapter forwards that internal name without mapping it to` AddToCart` .


Keep an explicit mapping between the business action and the outgoing TikTok event. Don't apply a general lowercase transformation to every destination.


Common mistakes include:


- **Lowercase names** , such as` purchase` , introduced by a normalization function.
- **Snake_case names** , such as` add_to_cart` , copied directly from an analytics event.
- **Names with spaces** , such as` Add To Cart` , copied from a human-readable label.
- **Custom purchase labels** , such as a store-specific checkout name, used where the team expects standard purchase reporting.


A custom purchase label may appear under its own name rather than contribute to the standard purchase event the analyst expects. Successful delivery doesn't prove correct classification.


### Check the deployed name, not just the specification


An event dictionary can be correct while the deployed tag is wrong. A template update may change a variable, or a server mapping may retain an old label after the browser code changes.


Inspect the actual browser hit and server payload. Compare the outgoing names character by character with the documented list.


After each tag or template change, compare names in both implementations. Keep the supported-events list as the reference rather than relying on memory or labels displayed in a tag manager.


## How to build server-side events for TikTok


Build the event around the saved business transaction, not around the page that displays it. The practical distinction in[server-side tracking](https://www.trackingplan.com/blog/server-side-tracking) is control over when an event is created, what it contains and how it survives delivery failures. If you send it from a server-side GTM container,[the guide to TikTok, Meta and Google Ads server-side](https://www.trackingplan.com/guides/server-side-tagging-meta-capi-google-ads-tiktok) covers the tags.


A diagram explaining three steps to build TikTok server-side events to avoid duplicate purchase data.


### Create a durable event before sending it


1.


**Reloads must not create purchases.** Generate` Purchase` after the order is saved, not when the confirmation page renders. The common slip is a page-refresh trigger that reports the same order again.


2.


**Retries need the original identity.** Persist the order or transaction identifier with the event record. A worker retry must reuse that record, not generate another order ID or purchase-event ID.


3.


**The occurrence time must survive queue delays.** Convert the saved transaction time to Unix seconds in UTC. Don't substitute the send time when a failed request returns to the queue.


4.


**Commerce fields must describe the saved order.** Validate` value` and` currency` together. Treat a` Purchase` with no value as an implementation error and hold it for correction rather than sending an incomplete commerce record.


5.


**Product reporting needs consistent identifiers.** Read` content_id` and the quantity from the same product source the storefront uses. Don't reconstruct them from confirmation-page text.


### Apply privacy controls before transmission


1.


**Raw contact details should not enter outgoing matching payloads.** Hash email and phone using **SHA-256** before sending them for matching, after normalising them: trim and lowercase the email, and write the phone in E.164 format (` +12133734253` ). Keep raw values out of request logs as well.


2.


**A server route doesn't override consent.** Send identifiers only when the applicable consent state permits them. Store that state with the event so the team can trace the basis for transmission.


3.


**Delivery needs an audit trail.** Post to` /event/track/` with the source fields and` data` array, then store the response beside the order ID. Distinguish a transport failure from an event-validation error so the worker doesn't retry a malformed payload indefinitely.


Use restricted logging for troubleshooting. Engineers need event identity, validation results and delivery status, not unrestricted copies of customer records.


A healthy result is a durable event linked to the order, a permitted payload and a stored response.


## Deduplicating TikTok Pixel and Events API conversions


The browser Pixel and server API aren't independent conversions when they report the same purchase. They're delivery paths for copies of the same business event.


[TikTok's web setup guidance](https://business-api.tiktok.com/portal/docs/events-api-v1-web-get-started/v1.3) recommends combining the TikTok Pixel with Events API and sharing events and parameters consistently. Without a shared deduplication signal, the same purchase can be counted twice.


### Separate deduplication from user matching


The event source ID links the copies to the same Pixel Code. The event name must match exactly. The` event_id` must identify the business event and remain identical across its browser and server copies.


**What each Purchase copy must carry for deduplication**


Signal Browser Pixel copy Server Events API copy Must match


` event_source_id` Pixel Code Same Pixel Code Yes


Event name` Purchase`` Purchase` Yes, exact casing


` event_id` Shared ID Same shared ID Yes, unique per event


Value and currency Order value and currency Same order value and currency Yes


` ttclid` Captured from the landing URL Passed from stored session Same value when present


Transaction identity Order ID Same order ID Yes


The table combines **deduplication keys** with **payload consistency and matching checks** . Value, currency and transaction identity should agree, but they don't replace the deduplication key.


The TikTok Click ID,` ttclid` , connects the event to click context. Preserve it through permitted landing-page storage, redirects and checkout handoffs. Advanced Matching, IP address and user-agent data help match web events to users; they serve a different purpose from deciding whether received hits represent the same event.


### Generate the identity once


Say the backend creates a purchase-event ID when it saves an order. It exposes that ID to the confirmation-page Pixel and uses the same stored ID in its Events API request.


That architecture gives both copies the same identity. By contrast, independently generating a random ID in each environment creates distinct events from TikTok's perspective.


A transaction ID can help derive the event identity, but define the event type as well. An order's purchase and a later business action aren't automatically the same event because they share an order record.


When investigating[CAPI deduplication issues](https://www.trackingplan.com/blog/capi-deduplication-issues) , inspect the actual outgoing IDs before changing reporting settings. On each release, verify that both purchase copies carry the same name, value, currency, transaction identity and` event_id` .


## Test matrix for proving deduplication works


Run the matrix against controlled business events and compare the expected count with the received hits and the Browser, Server and Server & Browser metrics on the pixel's detail page.


[TikTok's deduplication documentation](https://business-api.tiktok.com/portal/docs/event-deduplication/v1.3) identifies the event source ID, event name and` event_id` as deduplication inputs, and says duplicate Events API events can be removed when they arrive within a **48-hour window** . TikTok keeps the first event and discards the later copies, and a copy that arrives within 5 minutes has its data merged into the first one.


**Deduplication test matrix with expected counts**


Test case Expected count What to compare


Purchase, browser and server with the same` event_id` 1 counted TikTok-reported purchases against orders


Purchase, browser only 1 counted Pixel fires once per order confirmation


Purchase, server only 1 counted Server copy carries the same order ID


Purchase, server retry with the same` event_id` 1 counted Retry reuses the stored identity


AddToCart, overlapping delivery within 48 hours 1 counted Add-to-cart count per session


Lead from the CRM (custom event) and the same form submit from the Pixel 2 counted, different event sources Which pipeline owns the lead outcome


CRM lead sent through the API and uploaded as CSV with the same` event_id` 1 counted` event_id` in the payload and in the CSV row


Purchase,` event_id` generated separately in browser and backend 2 counted Duplicate persists; IDs differ


These are controlled test expectations, not guarantees that every delivered event becomes an attributed ad conversion. A CRM event never merges with a Pixel event: a CRM Event Set ID and a Pixel Code are different event sources, so matching` event_id` values don't help.


### Read the failure before choosing the fix


Compare raw browser and server hits, exact event names,` event_source_id` and` event_id` values, and timestamps against TikTok-reported conversions. Keep the underlying order or lead record beside that evidence.


**Doubled counts** suggest separately generated IDs, an unexpected source identity or another trigger. Check those possibilities before removing a delivery path.


**Dropped counts** require a different investigation. Check whether the browser path fired, whether the server created an event and whether a missing order ID caused your pipeline to reject or lose the record. A missing order ID isn't itself proof that TikTok discarded the hit.


For browser evidence, use the[TikTok Pixel Helper workflow](https://www.trackingplan.com/blog/tiktok-pixel-helper) , then pair its findings with server logs. Don't infer backend delivery from a working Pixel.


For` AddToCart` , isolate the intended action within the session. A customer can legitimately add products repeatedly, so session totals alone don't establish duplication.


## One conversion contract across web, app, offline and CRM


A business can have a correct web integration and inconsistent conversion reporting overall. The app team may define purchase value differently, the store export may use another order key, and the CRM may create new identities during import.


[TikTok's Events API 2.0 documentation](https://business-api.tiktok.com/portal/docs/events-api-2.0/v1.3) recommends the unified endpoint for web, app, offline and CRM reporting. Use that shared structure to enforce a common contract, not to assume automatic deduplication across source boundaries.


### Write rules that each source can check


The contract should define:


- **Event meaning.** Specify the business condition that qualifies as a purchase, registration or lead outcome.
- **Name and commerce fields.** Set the standard name, value calculation, currency rule and product identifier reference.
- **Transaction identity.** Preserve the order or lead ID through exports, imports and downstream updates.
- **Event identity.** Define how an` event_id` is created, persisted and reused for copies, while distinguishing different actions.
- **Consent and permitted identifiers.** Document which match keys may be sent for each consent state and region.


Hashing doesn't replace consent or a documented purpose. Define retention and access rules for the stored matching data as well.


### Migrate the record, not just the endpoint


Map each existing Events API 1.0 event to its 2.0 name and fields. Compare the mapping with actual records from the app, storefront, sales export and CRM.


Test an event from every active source before retiring the old call. Control overlapping migration traffic so the old and new pipelines don't create unplanned copies.


For offline and CRM records, preserve the order or lead ID that links the outcome to its originating web or app interaction. Pass stored` ttclid` and permitted Advanced Matching data when the record holds them.


Distinguish a **copy** from a **new outcome** . A CRM import of an existing purchase shouldn't become another purchase because the importer generated a new ID. A qualified lead, however, may represent a later business stage rather than a duplicate of the original form submission.


Shared business identity supports reconciliation, but cross-source deduplication still requires compatible source identity and delivery conditions. Where those conditions don't hold, choose which pipeline reports the conversion instead of relying on matching order IDs.


Assign a named team to own the contract. Every source change should pass that team's review before release.


## Validating conversion signals before the next campaign launch


Start with release evidence, not a dashboard total. A plausible conversion count can hide missing server events and duplicate browser triggers that happen to offset each other.


Use this release-week order:


1. **Confirm active sources.** Identify which sources the business sends and fix missing outcomes or undocumented pipelines.
2. **Check standard names.** Compare deployed event names with the supported-events list.
3. **Run controlled conversions.** Execute the deduplication matrix on a staging order and a live order after release.
4. **Schedule reconciliation.** Compare TikTok, GA4 and CRM results daily or weekly, with a written tolerance and a named reviewer.


This release check is one part of a wider[TikTok audit](https://www.trackingplan.com/blog/tiktok-audit) of the account and its data. Keep the launch checklist visible to the tag owner:


A checklist for validating conversion signals before launching a digital marketing campaign, shown in three steps.


### Reconcile definitions before totals


TikTok, GA4 and the CRM don't necessarily count the same population. Before calling a difference a tracking failure, align the event definition, reporting dates, timezone, attribution scope and treatment of cancelled orders.


Start with saved transactions and received events. Then examine which conversions each reporting system attributes to marketing. Don't force attributed purchases to equal every CRM order.


Record the reason for every accepted difference. A tolerance without a definition can turn a recurring implementation fault into a number the team stops investigating.


### Keep checking after the release


Track the share of paid landing sessions that retain` ttclid` through the relevant journey. Inspect the consent state attached to events, and verify that prohibited identifiers aren't sent when consent is refused.


After tag or template changes, look for duplicate triggers and missing properties. Inspect outgoing matching fields for unhashed email and phone values. A passing launch test doesn't prove that a later checkout or consent-manager release preserved the implementation.
